item.title: Akiyoshidai
item.description:
About

From https://tech-diving.jp/akiyoshidai

What is Akiyoshidai? Akiyoshidai is Japan’s largest karst plateau , located in the central and eastern parts of Mine City, Yamaguchi Prefecture. Its limestone distribution covers approximately 93 km², a scale unparalleled anywhere else in Japan.

More than 400 limestone caves have been identified in Akiyoshidai, including Akiyoshido Cave , one of Japan’s three largest limestone caves and a designated special natural monument.

Akiyoshidai is divided into two plateaus, Higashidai and Nishidai, by the Higashikawa River . Higashidai (Akiyoshidai in the narrow sense) was designated a national park (Akiyoshidai National Park) in 1955 and a special natural monument in 1964. In addition, individual caves are registered as natural monuments, and meticulous care is taken in their maintenance and management.

item.title: Algeria
item.description:
About

Algeria features a diverse landscape that includes mountain ranges, vast deserts, and karstic plateaus, making it highly relevant from a speleological and geological perspective.

🪨 Limestone Karst in Algeria

Yes, Algeria has significant limestone karst formations, especially in the northern and northeastern regions of the country. These include:

  • Djurdjura Mountains (part of the Tell Atlas): This region has well-developed karst plateaus with numerous caves and sinkholes, formed in Jurassic and Cretaceous limestones.
  • **Constantine and Setif regions**: Known for complex karst systems and underground hydrology.
  • Tassili n’Ajjer (southeastern Algeria - DO NOT TRAVEL): While primarily known for its sandstone formations and prehistoric rock art, some karst-like erosion features occur in isolated carbonate outcrops.

item.title: Allendale East Cave – Soggy Wombats
item.description:
Allendale East Cave

Introduction

Known as the hole in the middle of the road or just ‘the Dale’, Allendale East Cave is a very popular site among the CDAA Cave rated divers in the Mount Gambier region. As it presents itself as a non-complex cave to dive in, the Soggy Wombats Team has been training, developing skills and accumulating experience in this cave since 2019. Although geographically far from the most developed cave systems in the region, ‘the Dale’ has a small ‘tunnel’ at it’s deepest end that has been in most of Australian’s Cave Divers dreams to break into something big. There hasn’t been any breakthrough in this cave in the last 20 years or so, but with the advances in exploration techniques, we might be surprised with what the future will tell us.

item.title: Armenia
item.description:
About

Area of Interest: Vayots Dzor, Syunik, Tavush Moderate to High Cave Potential

  • Large parts of Armenia’s landscape are limestone and dolomite, particularly in the Vayots Dzor, Syunik, and Tavush provinces.
  • Features rugged terrain with karst valleys, dolines, and numerous caves, many of which are still actively being mapped by local and European caving groups.

Known Caves

  • Mozrov Cave, Magili Cave, and Arjeri Cave are significant dry caves.
  • Armenia is known for deep fissure systems and vertical caves — some of which contain seasonal sumps or intermittent water pools.

Cave Diving Status

  • No published records of cave diving expeditions.
  • Numerous karst springs, resurgences, and hydrothermal systems may offer dive potential, particularly at mid-altitudes where the water table is accessible.

Exploration Potential

  • High chance of discovering new phreatic or resurgence caves.
  • Requires satellite scouting and geological mapping to identify high-potential karst spring zones.
  • Local geology and hydrology suggest first-descent opportunities, especially during spring melt (April–June).

item.description:
Exploring Japan’s Hidden Rivers

An Australian cave diving expedition to the Mine–Akiyoshidai Karst Plateau Geopark By Josh Richards & Will Passos

Josh Richards and Will Passos walking through a bamboo forest after their first dive in Terayama Cave

The Mine–Akiyoshidai Karst Plateau Geopark in western Japan is famous for its limestone scenery, extensive cave systems and the enormous Akiyoshido tourist cave. However beneath it’s picturesque landscape, the Mine-Akiyoshidai plateau is riddled with submerged passages and an active groundwater system that remains only partially understood.

item.title: Article - Iddlebiddy Cave - Soggy Wombats - DRAFT
item.description:
Introduction

First discovered sometime in the early 1980’s by an enthusiastic band of unqualified local divers, Iddlebiddy Cave was named as a tongue-in-cheek nod to far larger Cocklebiddy Cave on the Nullarbor Plains which is resembles in structure if not in size. The location of Iddlebiddy Cave remained a closely guarded secret for several years, until it was first formally surveyed on 26 November 1988 by Tony Hambling, Frank Homewood and John McCormick on behalf of the Cave Divers Association of Australia.

item.description:
Reference: https://soggywombats.com.au/2024/04/15/making-sense-with-mnemo/

My v1 MNemo with a graphite pencil for note-taking

Like most folks stuck in Melbourne’s lockdown, I didn’t have much to get excited about during 2020. Having finished my cave course in late 2019 and then leaving Mount Gambier under less than ideal circumstances, all I could do was dream about was getting back to explore the caves I was finally qualified to get into. More than just diving and admiring them though, I desperately wanted to get back to try and understand Mount Gambier’s caves - why they’re shaped the way they are, understand how the different rock formations have developed, and (like every new and overly optimistic cave diver) hopefully use all of that to discover something new!

item.title: Article - What's Your ppO2
item.description: There’s one thing watched by rebreather divers with greater concern above anything else - your partial pressure of oxygen, aka “ppO2”. No matter how extraordinary it feels breathing warm air with no bubbles, clearing deco far quicker than your open circuit buddies and drifting around gently to the sound of your own breath; it all comes at the cost of knowing the gas in your loop can quickly and easily become toxic if you’re not vigilantly watching your ppO2. If a solenoid sticks open or a manual add valve jams on, the flood of oxygen into the loop can drive your ppO2 over 1.60 and quickly lead to a hyperoxic convulsion that will ruin your whole day. On the flip side we need a ppO2 of about 0.18atm - equivalent to 18% oxygen on the surface - just to maintain regular brain function, and about 0.15 to maintain consciousness. And as I was brutally reminded earlier this year, ppO2 also happens to drop rather rapidly just as you approach the surface when you think the dive is over.

item.title: Azerbaijan
item.description:
About

Moderate Potential Areas of Interest: Talysh and Caucasus Foothills

Geological Context

  • Azerbaijan has extensive limestone outcrops in the Greater Caucasus, Lesser Caucasus, and Talysh Mountains.
  • Karst formations are concentrated in Nakhchivan, Ismailli, and Lankaran areas.

Known Caves

  • Dry caves like Ashabi-Kahf, Karst caves of Gobustan, and others have archaeological and geological significance.
  • Thermal karst springs exist in Nakhchivan and other mountainous zones.

Cave Diving Status

  • No documented cave diving.
  • However, karst springs near Lankaran and Lerik may contain submerged sections suitable for exploration.

Exploration Potential

  • Greater logistical challenges and less existing infrastructure than Armenia.
  • Some springs in south-eastern Azerbaijan (Talysh Range) appear strong enough to support substantial submerged conduits.

Whip Cave? Runaway Cave?

Lost Lake Cave

  • Location: Western plateau, inland from Flying Fish Cove
  • Type: Partially flooded limestone cave
  • Details: Known to contain an underground lake with significant depth. The full extent of the submerged section has never been explored, but it is considered one of the most promising inland sites for potential cave diving.
  • Exploration Status: Dry portions mapped; no documented dive attempts.

Daniel Roux Cave

  • Location: Near the eastern coast, northeast of South Point
  • Type: Dry limestone cave with multiple chambers
  • Details: While primarily dry, reports mention water seepage and active flow in the wet season. Potential exists for deeper sections to be partially flooded.
  • Exploration Status: Surveyed, but no recorded underwater exploration.

The Dales

  • Location: Western coast, near Hugh’s Dale Waterfall
  • Type: Karst spring and stream system
  • Details: Features spring-fed water emerging from the base of limestone cliffs. The area around Hugh’s Dale and Anderson Dale may be connected to subterranean water systems—possible resurgence cave diving target.
  • Exploration Status: Surface features documented; no known underwater exploration.

Hosnies Spring Cave

  • Location: North coast, near Hosnies Spring
  • Type: Coastal karst feature with permanent spring
  • Details: This area features a freshwater spring discharging into a brackish mangrove environment, suggesting a potential coastal cave system or resurgence beneath.
  • Exploration Status: Caves reported nearby but not explored underwater.

Waterfall Cave / Runoff Sites (Unnamed)

  • Location: North-west coast cliffs between Martin Point and Ethel Beach
  • Type: Sea caves and freshwater outflows
  • Details: Rainfall channels sometimes discharge clear freshwater through cliffs, indicating potential connections to karst drainage systems that could be explored from the sea side via cave diving.
  • Exploration Status: Not documented or surveyed for cave access, but satellite imagery shows several sea-level notches.

Dolly Beach & Greta Beach Karst System

  • Location: South-east coast
  • Type: Cliff-edge karst with marine influence
  • Details: Both beaches are bordered by steep limestone with visible dissolution features. No documented caves, but the geological setting is favourable for sea cave development, possibly with partially submerged access.
  • Exploration Status: No known surveys, but suitable for scouting.

item.title: Goa Lalauwi
item.description:
About

From Anita: - This is a cave that deserves a special mention. A 600m submerged tunnel leads into the heart of the cave. So far around 3km of tunnels have been explored, yet the cave keeps on going. Goa Lalauwi keeps a few secrets up its sleeve as it wants you to come back for more. On my first dive we swam through big tunnels with white limestone, sections of fractured rock and large areas of stalagmites in crystal clear blue water. To get to the water you walk over 100 steps down a dry chamber which means the cave it self is never exposed to any sunlight. It’s pitch black. This means you are reliant on your torch as soon as you step into the cave. It is quite slippery at the entrance lake and you need to take care not to slip and fall. Then you kit up inside the lake aided by your torch light before the descent towards the first tunnel. The second dive in this beauty was far more complex from a navigational perspective with lots of directional decisions and several jumps that lead to a section with little white humps in the form of witches’ hats. According to our guide, these formations are considered quite rare and, unlike the other speleothems in the caves, form under water. While I have spent several hours in this cave, I will be back for more.

About

Go June to September? (Summer)

  • Calmest Weather & Longest Days:
    Iceland experiences milder weather, longer daylight hours (up to 24 hours near the solstice), and calmer surface conditions during summer. This makes logistics easier and safer, particularly when accessing remote dive sites.
  • Better Accessibility:
    Many of Iceland’s cave dive sites are in remote highland regions or near lava fields — during winter and spring, snow and ice can make these areas impassable. Roads are generally fully open by mid-June and remain accessible until early autumn.
  • Consistent Water Temperatures:
    Iceland’s groundwater-fed cave systems (like those at Silfra and Davíðsgjá) maintain constant temperatures year-round (~2–4°C), so water temps aren’t your limiting factor — surface conditions and access are.
  1. Silfra Fissure (Þingvellir National Park)
    • While not a cave in the traditional sense, Silfra offers crystal-clear visibility (~100m) in a tectonic fissure between the North American and Eurasian plates.
    • Accessible year-round, but summer offers the best overall experience due to comfort during gear changes and travel ease.
  2. Davíðsgjá
    • A darker, slightly deeper alternative to Silfra with limited overhead sections.
    • Best dived in summer for similar reasons — ease of access and surface comfort.
  3. Litlaá Lava Tube Cave Systems (near Lake Mývatn)
    • Actual underwater lava tube systems, rare and remote.
    • These are less developed for tourism and require expedition-level planning.
    • Only realistically accessible between July and early September.

Avoid October to May

item.description:
About

Kenya features both limestone karst landscapes and opportunities for cave diving, particularly along its coastal regions.

🪨 Limestone Karst in Kenya

Kenya’s coastal areas, notably around Vipingo in Kilifi County, are characterized by coralline limestone formations that have undergone karstification. These processes have led to the development of features such as caves, sinkholes, and underground voids. For instance, studies at the Vipingo Coral Limestone Quarry have documented various karst features and associated geohazards, including cavities and fissures in the rock mass. (ej-geo.org)

item.title: Palau
item.description:
About

Best time to go is May (Rubens) Palau offers year-round diving, but the dry season from October to May is considered the best time to visit. During this period, divers can expect calmer seas, better visibility (often exceeding 30 meters), and a higher likelihood of encountering diverse marine life.

Palau’s Rock Islands, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, are characterized by uplifted coral limestone formations that have been sculpted over millions of years by natural processes such as erosion, tidal action, and sea-level changes. This has resulted in a stunning karst topography featuring mushroom-shaped islands, caves, sinkholes, and underground channels. These formations are not only geologically significant but also contribute to the rich biodiversity and unique ecosystems found in the region

Why: Volcanic island with isolated limestone bands and possible lava tubes intersecting freshwater lenses.

  • Status: Known dry caves and lava tubes, but freshwater cave diving is almost nonexistent.
  • Potential: Search for anchialine pools or submerged karst pockets inland or near coastal freshwater springs.
  • Best Season: May to October (dry season).

Caves

  • Source de la Rivière Sainte-Suzanne, -20.9065, 55.6017, Strong resurgence on eastern slopes; spring-fed river emerging from volcanic fissure.
  • Source Bras Cabot (Salazie Cirque), -21.0003, 55.5376, High-altitude spring at base of basalt cliffs; potentially linked to perched aquifer system.
  • Source de la Rivière des Roches, -21.0084, 55.6661, Powerful spring from fractured basalt; popular canyoning area with high discharge.
  • Source du Bras de Cilaos, -21.1422, 55.4749, Resurgence below vertical cliffs in Cilaos cirque; likely fracture-controlled groundwater flow.
  • Takamaka Valley Spring, -21.0431, 55.6356, Remote and high-flow spring at base of volcanic wall; difficult access, high potential for unexplored source conduit.
  • Source de Grand Galet (Langevin Falls), -21.2856, 55.7083, Large spring-fed cascade; major discharge from volcanic plateau into Langevin River.
  • Source de Bras d’Annette, -21.0624, 55.6078, Spring in upper Takamaka basin; steep terrain with high groundwater flow potential.
  • Source de Bras Patience, -21.1187, 55.6081, Perennial spring from cliffside in upper Ravine Blanche; minor but consistent discharge.
  • Source Ravine Citron Galet, -21.1396, 55.6362, Emergent spring in deep ravine near Grand Étang; high rainfall recharge zone.
  • Source de la Plaine des Palmistes, -21.1123, 55.6379, Widespread seepage and spring outflows on elevated plateau; volcanic aquifer discharge zone.

item.title: Rwanda
item.description:
HIGH RISK - ALL KNOWN KARST <10KM FROM Democratic Republic of Congo

About

Karst around Bugarama and Nyungwe Forest

  • Why: Karst features in the southwest near the Congo border, with known limestone outcrops.
  • Status: Almost no documented speleology or diving.
  • Potential: Blue holes and flooded sinkholes possibly linked to geothermal springs.
  • Best Season: June to September (Long Dry season)

Why June to September?

  • Dry Conditions:
    Rwanda has two dry seasons — the long dry season (June to September) and a shorter one (December to February). The long dry season offers the most stable weather, lowest rainfall, and easiest overland travel, which is essential when accessing remote or undeveloped cave sites.
  • Reduced Flood Risk:
    In karst systems, dry seasons reduce the chance of sudden flooding, improve visibility, and lower flow rates in submerged passages — critical factors for safe cave diving.
  • Cool but Comfortable Climate:
    Rwanda’s elevation means temperatures are generally mild year-round (20–27°C in the day), but the dry season offers the most reliable surface conditions for expedition logistics.

Important Cave Diving Context for Rwanda

  • Emerging or Untapped Potential:
    Rwanda is not currently a mainstream cave diving destination, but it does have significant volcanic and karst features — especially around the Northwest (Musanze) and Western regions (near Lake Kivu and Nyungwe Forest). Several lava tube caves like Musanze Caves exist, and while most are explored on foot, they may include submerged sections not yet fully mapped.
  • Exploratory Diving:
    Any cave diving in Rwanda is likely to be exploratory in nature, potentially requiring permits, environmental approvals, and collaboration with local authorities or researchers.
  • Access & Logistics:
    Remote locations, lack of existing dive infrastructure, and the potential need for self-supported expeditions (including rebreathers or portable compressors) make timing your trip for the dry season even more important.

Other Considerations

  • Permits & Conservation:
    Rwanda is extremely conservation-focused — engaging with the Rwanda Development Board (RDB) or local geologists would be essential for any diving expedition.
  • Rainy Season (March–May, October–November):
    Avoid these months. Roads may become impassable, visibility drops, and cave flooding becomes a serious risk.

1. Musanze Region (Northern Province)

  • Geological Features: This area is characterized by extensive lava tubes formed from ancient volcanic activity, particularly from the Bisoke and Sabyinyo volcanoes.
  • Notable Caves:
    • Musanze Caves: Approximately 2 km long with 31 known entrances, these caves are part of the lava basaltic layers and are the most frequently visited in Rwanda.
    • Ubuvumo Bwibihonga: The longest cave in Rwanda, featuring a multi-level system of parallel lava tubes.
  • Exploration Potential: While these caves are primarily known for dry exploration, the presence of lava tubes suggests potential for submerged sections, especially during the rainy season when water levels rise. (Visit Rwanda)

2. Nyungwe Forest Region (Western Rwanda)

  • Geological Features: This region is part of the Albertine Rift and is characterized by ancient Precambrian rocks, including quartzite and schist. While traditional karst formations are less common here, the area’s complex geology may host unique subterranean features.
  • Exploration Potential: Limited information is available about caves in this region, suggesting an opportunity for pioneering exploration.

The northwestern and western parts of Rwanda, particularly near the Volcanoes National Park and along the Albertine Rift, contain limestone and dolomitic formations associated with the uplifted sedimentary sequences of the rift system.

item.description:
import json
import requests
import csv
import time

API_KEY = 'YOUR GOOGLE API'  # Replace with your API key

# Keywords likely to return cave/sinkhole/bathing spring results
KEYWORDS = [
    'goa', 'gua', 'lubang', 'sumur alam', 'serambi alam',
    'lembah', 'grotto', 'cave', 'hole',
    'loji', 'koo', 'luban', 'permandian'
]

# Approximate coverage of Muna Island
TILE_LOCATIONS = [
    '-4.783,122.566',  # Raha
    '-5.000,122.500',  # Southwest
    '-4.600,122.700',  # Northeast
    '-4.900,122.700'   # Southeast
]

RADIUS = 50000  # 50km radius — max allowed
OUTPUT_CSV = 'muna_island_places.csv'

def search_places(keyword, location, radius, token=None):
    url = 'https://maps.googleapis.com/maps/api/place/nearbysearch/json'
    params = {
        'key': API_KEY,
        'keyword': keyword,
        'location': location,
        'radius': radius,
    }
    if token:
        params['pagetoken'] = token
  
    response = requests.get(url, params=params)
    return response.json()
  
def collect_all_places():
    all_results = [] 
    for location in TILE_LOCATIONS:
        for keyword in KEYWORDS:
            print(f"Searching for '{keyword}' near {location}")
            data = search_places(keyword, location, RADIUS)
            all_results.extend(data.get('results', []))
  
            while 'next_page_token' in data:
                time.sleep(2)
                token = data['next_page_token']
                data = search_places(keyword, location, RADIUS, token)
                all_results.extend(data.get('results', []))
  
    # Deduplicate by place_id
    deduped = {place['place_id']: place for place in all_results}
    return list(deduped.values())
  
def save_to_csv(places, filename):
    fieldnames = ['name', 'address', 'latitude', 'longitude', 'types', 'place_id']
    with open(filename, 'w', newline='', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fieldnames)
        writer.writeheader()
        for place in places:
            writer.writerow({
                'name': place.get('name'),
                'address': place.get('vicinity'),
                'latitude': place['geometry']['location']['lat'],
                'longitude': place['geometry']['location']['lng'],
                'types': ', '.join(place.get('types', [])),
                'place_id': place.get('place_id')
            })
  
if __name__ == '__main__':
    results = collect_all_places()
    save_to_csv(results, OUTPUT_CSV)
    print(f"\nSaved {len(results)} unique places to '{OUTPUT_CSV}'")

Where it is & what it is
On the WA Nullarbor near Cocklebiddy; entrance on the lip of a doline with a long haul down to water. Expect a dry entrance slope through breakdown to a lake, then multiple sumps and at least one intervening airspace.

  • Steep entrance → main chamber → lake → ~190 m sump through a phreatic maze → large dry chamber (~80 m) with another lake at far end. item.title: Tonga
item.description:
About

Best time is April to October (Dry season). Excellent visibility and the chance to encounter humpback whales during their migration (June to November).

Tonga’s geological landscape includes islands with uplifted coral limestone formations, leading to the development of karst topography characterized by caves, sinkholes, and underground drainage systems. Notably, ʻEua Island exhibits extensive limestone formations with karst features, including numerous caves formed through the dissolution of carbonate rocks.

item.title: Tunisia
item.description:
About

🪨 Limestone Karst and Caves in Tunisia

Tunisia’s karst topography is primarily found in its central and western regions, characterized by extensive limestone and dolomite formations. These areas host numerous caves formed through karstification processes.(geologyscience.com)

  • Djebel Serj: Located in central Tunisia, this limestone mountain is home to significant cave systems, including the Ain Dhab and Mine caves. The Mine Cave is considered the longest in Tunisia, extending over 4 kilometers. (en.wikipedia.org, en.wikipedia.org)
  • Jebel Bargou: Adjacent to Djebel Serj, this area also features karstic formations with caves developed in Aptian limestone. (en.wikipedia.org)
  • Cave Nefza: Situated in the northwest, this cave extends approximately 310 meters and showcases various speleothems. (en.wikipedia.org)

These karst systems are significant both geologically and hydrologically, contributing to the region’s groundwater resources. (link.springer.com)
